newsitem.title: UK: HSBC shares up as figures beat forecasts.
newsitem.headline: HSBC shares up as figures beat forecasts.

text.p: Shares in HSBC Holdings Plc, one of the world's biggest financial services groups, jumped on Monday after the bank announced profits and dividends ahead of expectations.
Pre-tax profit in sterling terms rose 13 percent to 2.623 billion pounds ($4.3 billion) while the first half dividend was up 33 percent to 20 pence per share.
Analysts had forecast pre-tax profits of between 2.32 and 2.48 billion pounds.
HSBC shares, which were lower ahead of the announcement, jumped to a high of 2326p before settling 86p higher at 2279.5p by late morning.

HSBC's chairman Sir William Purves said the group had increased attributable profit to 1.757 billion pounds, 11 percent ahead of the comparable figure in 1996 "despite the adverse exchange rate translation impact of stronger sterling" thought to have cut profits by around 70 million pounds.
Purves said HSBC would consolidate recent acquisitions in Latin America before moving on elsewhere but noted banking assets in mature markets look expensive.

"We don't have a shopping list, we look at opportunities all round the world as we've done and followed through in Latin America," Purves said. "We're not active in this field, we've done quite a lot this year and we'll see that consolidate before we get excited about other things."
Purves said in an interview he was not against investing in relatively mature markets on principle.
He noted, for example, that Marine Midland continues to buy when the price is right in the United States.
"Some of the prices I see, and the premiums you would have to pay for banks in some of these mature markets, I don't think would be in the best interests of our shareholders," Purves said.
The HSBC chairman said the board will address the subject of excess capital when the bank believes it cannot invest it.
"Our business continues to grow...we're not short of lending opportunities. We don't feel that the opportunities in the group are such that we can't use the capital."
He said the dividend rise, which was greater than analysts had expected, was a function of the bank's policy of making the interim payout a larger proportion of the full year.
"I don't think anybody should be thinking that the full-year dividend will be 33 percent up," Purves said.

HSBC's tier one ratio dipped to 9.4 percent at the half year from 9.9 percent at the end of last year due to its investment in Latin America but Purves noted that the underlying trend was for capital to be generated strongly.
"We've increased the dividend a bit, so you can read into that that we're aware of the capital growth," he said.
HSBC owns HongKong Bank in the Far East, Midland Bank in the UK, and its HSBC America's unit includes Marine Midland. It also has a controlling stake in Hang Seng Bank.

Noting that all units had done well, Purves said HongKong Bank's results had been affected by a significant underwriting loss at its investment banking subsidiary about which he declined to give any details.
HSBC reported growth in loans especially in Hong Kong, where the property market was buoyant, and in the UK where corporate and mortgage lending was up.
Purves said the Hong Kong market was very competitive with margins narrowing in the mortgage market but added that the bank had maintained its market share.
He said that margins were under pressure at Midland Bank as well though the bank had managed a sharp fall in cost income ratio.
Group net interest margin actually improved from 2.91 percent at the year-end to 2.94 at the half-year with pressures offset by higher margin business in Brazil.
In group costs, cost to income ratio improved slightly to 52.4 percent from 52.6 percent with its acquisition of Banco HSBC Bamerindus in Brazil adding two points to the figure.
Purves said currency turmoil in the Far East in recent months had not generated significant profits or losses but had added to volumes and volatility.
Purves said it was "business as usual" in Hong Kong since the territory was taken over by China, adding that the bank has complete confidence in Hong Kong's development.

He said HSBC was also pleased with progress in mainland China although he conceded this was slow and that foreign banks are probably not the Chinese government's main priority in terms of development.
